Positive equity can still fail a collateral test: separate repayment, new collateral and a sale

Chart a fictional loan-to-collateral limit, compare two outside-resource adjustments, and calculate how an internal sale changes both the loan and its collateral.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep positive equity separate from a hypothetical loan-to-collateral test

Interactive planning lab

Collateral value less debt at the selected stress$20,000
Outside cash to repay debt to the fictional limit$8,000
Additional eligible collateral if debt stays unchanged$13,333.33

Original static nominal-CAD collateral illustration. This fictional contract tests debt divided by eligible collateral against the entered maximum ratio. The limit is not a CIRO, FINRA, legal or lender requirement. All entered collateral receives full eligibility value with no haircut; it falls instantly by the selected percentage. Debt stays fixed until the illustrated adjustment, with no interest, fees, tax, price slippage or intervening transactions. The selected loan-to-collateral ratio is 71.43%. External repayment reduces debt while keeping this collateral fixed. Posting additional eligible collateral leaves debt fixed. Both use resources outside the initially entered collateral pool and are alternative mathematical cases, not costs to add together or rights under an actual agreement. Under the same fictional terms, selling CAD 20,000 of existing collateral and using all proceeds immediately to repay debt would meet the test, leaving CAD 50,000 of collateral and CAD 30,000 of debt. No response deadline, sale price, extension, acceptable deposit or ability to transact is promised. Actual contracts and eligibility can differ or change.

The central idea

An account can have positive equity and still exceed a contractual debt ratio. Repaying debt, posting eligible collateral and selling assets to repay debt are different calculations.

01

Separate the amount you own from the ratio the contract tests

Suppose eligible collateral starts at CAD 100,000 and the loan outstanding is CAD 50,000. The entered pool initially has CAD 50,000 of equity and a 50% loan-to-collateral ratio. Those two descriptions use the same balance sheet, but they answer different questions.

Now apply an immediate 30% collateral-price decline, with the debt unchanged. Collateral falls to CAD 70,000, leaving CAD 20,000 after subtracting the loan. Equity is still positive. Yet the debt ratio is CAD 50,000 ÷ CAD 70,000, or about 71.43%.

The teaching contract permits a maximum ratio of 60%, so this case fails its test before equity reaches zero. That 60% is an original fictional input, not a margin requirement, an actual lender quote or a Canadian regulatory rule. The tool is a static cash-and-collateral illustration rather than an approval or enforcement model.

02

Locate the collateral threshold without assigning a probability to the loss

If debt is D and the maximum allowed debt ratio is c, the collateral value required by this particular test is D ÷ c. At the defaults, CAD 50,000 ÷ 60% gives CAD 83,333.33. Starting from CAD 100,000, a decline beyond about 16.67% crosses that threshold if nothing else changes.

That percentage is a mathematical price boundary, not the chance of a call or a forecast drawdown. The chart varies an immediate decline while keeping debt fixed. A real loan can include other tests, valuation rules, interest accrual and changes in eligible assets that are outside this formula.

The tool also permits a starting case that already exceeds the chosen limit. In that case, no further market decline is needed for the fictional test to fail. It does not imply that a lender would have approved those initial balances.

03

Outside repayment changes the numerator

With CAD 70,000 of collateral and a 60% limit, permitted debt is CAD 42,000. An outside cash repayment of CAD 8,000 reduces the original CAD 50,000 loan to that amount. The collateral stays CAD 70,000 and the ratio becomes 60%.

The formula is max(0, D − cV), where V is the stressed collateral value. This method changes debt while holding collateral fixed. It does not require a collateral sale within the entered pool, but it does require cash from somewhere outside it.

Repayment is not a second investment loss. If a household uses its own outside cash, its cash and debt both fall by the same amount before fees or tax effects. Equity inside this particular pool rises from CAD 20,000 to CAD 28,000, while outside cash falls by CAD 8,000. The transfer does not create household wealth.

04

Additional eligible collateral changes the denominator

If the debt instead remains CAD 50,000, total eligible collateral must rise to CAD 83,333.33. Starting from CAD 70,000, the additional amount is therefore CAD 13,333.33, assuming the new collateral receives its full stated value.

The formula is max(0, D ÷ c − V). It differs from the repayment formula because the denominator changes while debt stays fixed. At a 60% limit, one additional dollar of eligible collateral supports only 60 cents of debt capacity in this fictional test.

Posting an outside asset moves it into the committed collateral pool. The asset remains owned in this model, but its availability for another bill has changed. It is not income, an expense equal to its entire posted value or newly created wealth. Actual eligibility, haircuts, transfer timing and acceptance must come from an actual agreement; the calculator assumes them only for its stated example.

05

An internal sale changes both numerator and denominator

A third mathematical method sells some of the existing collateral and applies all proceeds immediately to the loan. If the sale amount is s, the new ratio is (D − s) ÷ (V − s). Subtracting s from the debt alone would miss the collateral leaving the pool.

Solving for the amount that reaches the limit gives s = (D − cV) ÷ (1 − c) when the test is initially breached and a partial-sale solution exists. At the defaults, that is CAD 8,000 ÷ 40%, or CAD 20,000. The remaining collateral is CAD 50,000, debt is CAD 30,000 and the ratio is 60%.

Before costs, the pool’s equity remains CAD 20,000 because both assets and debt fell by the same CAD 20,000. Exposure is smaller, and future gains or losses apply to fewer assets. This method does not have the same resource path as contributing CAD 8,000 of outside cash or CAD 13,333.33 of outside collateral.

If debt is at least the collateral value, no partial sale can restore a positive-collateral active loan ratio below 100% in this model. Selling everything either closes both balances when they are equal or leaves debt unpaid when debt is larger. The live assumptions state which case applies instead of showing a negative residual collateral balance as a workable solution.

06

Read the response bars as alternatives, not charges to add together

The grouped bars compare outside repayment with an outside collateral addition at several price stresses. Their different heights are a consequence of the different equations. They are not two amounts due together, nor do they prove that either resource is available to the household.

The matrix then changes the fictional ratio limit as well as the price decline. A tighter limit can increase the cash needed even at the same asset price and debt. The equity bridge, by contrast, is unchanged when only the limit changes. A contract test and a balance-sheet loss remain separate dimensions.

A response amount should therefore be matched to actual access to funds. An asset already assigned to another goal cannot also be counted as free collateral, and an unused borrowing limit does not establish that cash will remain available during the same stress.

07

Bring the actual agreement and transaction timing back into the plan

The SEC’s Investor.gov margin-account bulletin explains, in its U.S. investor-education context, that borrowing against securities can require additional funds or asset sales when prices decline. It also describes firm actions and changing requirements. This guide uses that source for broad risk context and does not reproduce its regulatory thresholds as this model’s contract.

The four charts assume a constant debt balance, immediate execution at entered values, fully eligible collateral, and no interest, tax, fees, slippage or price movement during an adjustment. They do not grant a right to select a response, promise a deadline or extension, or determine what a lender can accept or sell.

  1. Read the actual debt-ratio definition and eligible-value rules.
  2. Check when debt, interest and collateral are measured.
  3. Separate a cash repayment from a collateral transfer or internal sale.
  4. Identify available outside resources without counting them twice.
  5. Test the household’s bill payments alongside any contractual funding demand.

The result is a transparent set of conditional calculations. A workable borrowing plan still requires the actual terms and a cash path that can be executed when needed.
